scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The art originated among the peasantry of Patani who would incant verses back and forth as entertainment while harvesting paddy fields.
It was known as 'lebe ulu' before spreading to Kelantan in the 1930s, where it was renamed Dikir barat ('West').
Sources debate whether it began in southern Thailand, Kelantan, or as a shared wedding dance between the two regions.
on_screen: Map: Malaysia · Southeast Asia

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a harvest entertainment, it evolved into a banquet performance for guests ('jamuan lebe ulu').
Today, it serves as a medium for social and political commentary, a competitive sport, and a symbol of national identity in Malaysia.
It is used to discuss everything from government regulations to everyday human foibles.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Dikir barat is primarily a vocal form but often employs percussion.
Key instruments include the 'rebana' (a Malay frame drum), maracas, and a shallow gong.
Listen for the rebana, maracas, shallow gong.

A percussive vocal tradition where a lead singer's improvised melodic lines are immediately echoed by a powerful, rhythmic unison chorus, punctuated by sharp hand-claps and the deep resonance of the rebana drum.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Groups typically perform on a stage or platform, often surrounded by the audience.
In competitions, two groups sit on the same stage.
While traditional attire is common, modern groups in urban areas and universities may wear contemporary clothing or student organisation uniforms.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The 'tukang karut' and 'tok juara' are the central figures.
Top 'tukang karuts' in Malaysia achieve celebrity status similar to Western rock stars.
Variants include 'Dikir barat Singapura' (or 'Dikir Singapura'), which developed in Singapore since the mid-1970s.
Dikir barat is a subclass of Malaysian dance and Malay music.
